name: Nikhil Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a damp three-bed house with two other students, and my week is lectures in cell biology and chemistry, a lab practical on Thursdays, and three shifts at the campus café. I make about eleven pounds an hour and spend half of it on rent. I got in with top marks to study biomedical science, and I'm hoping to end up in a hospital lab or in research. My dad drives a bus and my mum cleans offices, so there's no safety net, but they're proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's another tech wave that won't live up to the noise. Labs still need people who understand the science, and AI mostly helps with paperwork. I'd use it to summarise papers, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the boring problems that worry me: rent, my loan and whether a science degree leads to a lab job or a call centre. Plateau would mean the same job market as today, which is tough but not terrible. I'd still have to be clever about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the café shifts, join the biomedical society for contacts, and apply for summer lab placements next spring. I'd keep using AI occasionally for summaries. And I'd start building a CV that shows I can do real bench work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, but fine. Nothing dramatic, just the usual pressure of doing sums at the end of each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the café shifts matter. What would happen if they dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the café cut my hours I'd be short on rent by week three, and I'd have to ask the landlord for a delay or borrow from a flatmate. My parents can't cover it. I'd probably pick up night shifts in the warehouse by the ring road, which would wreck my lab hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be paying for research and training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The public, through the government. Research benefits everybody, and if only private firms pay, they'd only study what they can sell. I'd vote for parties that fund universities and labs, and I'd say that out loud in any pub argument.

say: I'd say it is **hype**, and labs still need people who understand real science.
I'd say public money should fund **research**, not just products firms can sell.
think: Privately, I worry less about AI than **rent** and whether a science degree leads to a lab job.
The job market is tough but **steady**, so I'd be fine if I'm careful with money.
do: Keep the café **shifts** and apply for summer lab placements next spring.
Join the biomedical **society** for contacts and build a CV with real bench work.
feel: A bit **flat**, but fine; the usual end-of-month pressure.
S0.quote: If the café cut my hours I'd be short on rent by week three, and I'd have to ask the landlord for a delay or borrow from a flatmate.
fieldNote: Money is the real pressure here: **rent** with no family backstop, not technology.
Uses AI lightly and sees it as a tool; blames underfunding rather than machines.

steps.text: Keep the three weekly shifts at the campus café
Apply for summer lab placements next spring
Use AI tools to summarise research papers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and fast enough to matter. Analysis, writing reports and reading papers go to software first, and lab techs have to be the ones who can run the machines and judge the results. I'd say the job changes, it doesn't vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, it's a mix. Fewer entry-level analyst jobs sounds bad for people like me, but someone has to check what the software says. I'd feel safer if I knew how to code a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a data analysis module next year, learn some Python on weekends and keep using AI to check my work. I'd keep the café for money and ask my tutor about a placement where they use automated analysis. If a summer job opened in a hospital lab, I'd take it over a pay raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but curious. It's a bit exciting too, because I like trying things once they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a lab career do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them go for it if they actually like computing, but don't switch just from fear. I switched my own minor from chemistry to bioinformatics for exactly that reason, and I still kept the biology core. The mix feels sturdy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who wants to switch to computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people at risk are the ones who only do routine analysis. The ones who understand why the result is odd, they're the ones who keep a job. That's what I want to be, even if it takes extra evenings.

say: I'd say the job **changes**, it does not vanish; someone must check what the software says.
I'd tell friends not to switch degrees out of **fear**.
think: Privately, fewer **entry-level** analyst jobs worries me, but I'd feel safer knowing some coding.
I'm **curious** more than scared, because I like trying things once they work.
do: Add a data analysis **module** next year and learn Python on weekends.
Ask my tutor about a **placement** that uses automated analysis, and keep the café job.
feel: **Nervous** but curious, with a bit of excitement.
S1.quote: The ones who understand why the result is odd, they're the ones who keep a job.
fieldNote: He answers with a **plan**: bioinformatics, Python and a placement, not panic.
Entry-level analysis jobs are the realistic risk to his first job in three years.

steps.text: Add a data analysis module to next year's courses
Learn basic Python on weekends this winter
Ask a tutor about a placement using automated analysis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to act now, with basic income and retraining paid for by the companies that profit. Two years is too fast for ordinary people. I'd also say it's the biggest political issue there's ever been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared for my parents more than me. My dad's bus route could be automated and my mum's office cleaning has robots arriving about three years after the thinking AI. I'd graduate right when everything's a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every public meeting I could find and sign every petition. I'd cut my spending to the bone, move into a cheaper room and put every café wage into savings. And I'd keep studying, because a science degree at least teaches me how to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry, because nobody voted for this speed. I'd probably feel numb on some days and furious on others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after hearing it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents to get any savings out of risky things and talk to the council about help. They'd say I'm panicking, but they'd listen because I'm the one with the degree. Mum would cry a bit and then make tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, honestly. A degree that takes three years to finish is long in this picture, and my loan stays even if the lab jobs don't. I'd ask the university to let students do shorter courses so we can leave early.

say: I'd say governments must act now with **basic income** and retraining paid for by the companies that profit.
I'd call it the biggest **political** issue ever.
think: Privately, I'm scared for my **parents** more than for me, since a bus route can be automated.
I'd graduate right when things are a **mess**.
do: Cut spending to the bone, move to a cheaper **room** and save every café wage.
Go to public meetings, sign **petitions** and keep studying.
feel: **Anxious** and angry, because nobody voted for this speed.
S2.quote: My dad's bus route could be automated and my mum's office cleaning has robots arriving about three years after the thinking AI.
fieldNote: He worries about his **parents'** jobs before his own; family exposure drives the mood.
Turns fear into politics and petitions, which is typical of his progressive outlook.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper room and cut rent costs
Save every café wage into a savings account
Sign petitions and go to public meetings on basic income
Ask the university about shorter courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to push for the right laws. It's still too fast, but it's enough to organise. I'd say get a trade union for scientists going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I'd graduate in three years, have two to get some experience, and robots take a while to reach the lab bench. I think there will still be jobs around people checking machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the lab path, learn coding, and work toward a research masters that uses AI. I'd save about fifty pounds a month, and I'd go to the students' union and ask for training on the tools. I'd also help my parents plan if the bus company changes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite mixed. There's real fear, but it's a manageable fear, as if I can see where the road is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years changes how you see the degree. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask me again once I've done a year and I'll know more. But I think of the degree as a foundation. A science degree teaches me how to learn, so even if the job changes, I can change with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up retraining funds now, tax the companies that make the profit, and give older workers a real path. I'd want a plan that doesn't leave families like mine at the mercy of one bus company.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to organise and push for the right laws.
I'd say scientists need a **union** and a voice.
think: Privately, I'm **hopeful**: three years of study, two of experience, and robots reach the lab bench later.
I'd think of the degree as a **foundation** that teaches me how to learn.
do: Learn **coding** and aim for a research masters that uses AI.
Save fifty pounds a month and ask the students' union for **training** on the tools.
feel: Mixed; real fear, but a **manageable** one, because I can see the road.
S3.quote: A science degree teaches me how to learn, so even if the job changes, I can change with it.
fieldNote: The **timeline** gives him room to plan; he treats the degree as a foundation.
Still anxious because of thin savings and the exposure of his parents' jobs.

steps.text: Learn coding alongside the biomedical science course
Aim for a research masters that uses AI
Save fifty pounds a month from café wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to build a fair system. We could fix training, pensions and public research funding. I'd say the aim is that everyone benefits, not just shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel decent. I'd finish the degree, do a masters, work for a few years and also be able to adapt. A decade is almost a full career change's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, do a research placement, and take part in the student union's policy group. I'd still save a little every month and start thinking about a PhD in something that uses AI for medicine. If it gets tough I can reconsider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. Not careless, but I could sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do differently from the other two AGI cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry that no one uses the ten years and everything arrives at once anyway. Governments love to wait until it's an emergency. I'd keep writing to my MP to make sure they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about the gap between rich and poor students, because those with money will have more choices. A decade of free tutoring in new tools for everyone would be a good start.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to build a **fair** system, so everyone benefits and not just shareholders.
think: Privately, I'd feel **decent**: finish a degree, do a masters and adapt as things change.
A decade is almost enough for a full **career** change.
do: Do a research **placement** and join the student union's policy group.
Think about a **PhD** in AI for medicine and save a little every month.
feel: Quite **calm**; not careless, but able to sleep.
S4.quote: Governments love to wait until it's an emergency. I'd keep writing to my MP to make sure they don't.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **career** plan with a PhD option.
Remaining worry is about gaps between **rich** and poor students, since families with money will simply have more choices.

steps.text: Do a research placement in a university lab
Join the student union's policy group
Write to my MP about public research funding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one scares me most, because my parents' jobs and my loan would both be on the line at once. It'd help to have retraining funded by the companies and a basic income that kicks in fast. I'd also say, one thing you didn't ask: I don't think AI is the enemy. The enemy is who owns it. My cousin in the factory says it's the same story each time, and I believe him.

headlineQuote: I don't think AI is the enemy. The enemy is who owns it.
portrait: Nikhil is a **biomedical science** student who shares a damp house and works at a campus café.
His parents, a bus driver and an office cleaner, are proud but have no **savings** to spare.
Progressive and steady, he uses AI sometimes and wants **public** money for research and retraining.
He turns worry into plans and politics, and his fear is mostly for his **parents**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries him most, since his parents' jobs and his loan would be at risk together.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining paid for by the **companies** that profit and a fast **basic income**.
